title: What is known about 1RB1RE_1LC0RC_1RA1LD_1RB0LA_0LC1RF_---1RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RE_1LC0RC_1RA1LD_1RB0LA_0LC1RF_---1RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine runs a base-4 counter at the left end of the tape: digits a, b, ab, bb (0 to 3) separated by long blocks of pairs ba, incremented once per excursion of the head, and every block shrinks by two pairs per cycle of the digit after it (a countdown timer). The digit rules are proved in Lean for all block lengths. Lean also shows that tapes of the same shape with short blocks halt, so nonhalting cannot follow from the shape alone: it depends on the block lengths the run from blank tape produces. No halt in 1011 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 57,981 cells have been visited and 43,904 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.506). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.063).

claims.title: The digit rules
claims.text: At the left end the tape is D> 0 b (ba)^n1 s1 (ba)^n2 s2 ...; one excursion of the head increments the first separator: a → b, ab → bb (c1, any tape to the right), b → ab with one pair moving from the right block to the left block (c2), and bb → a with a carry into the next separator a or b (c4, c5), for all block lengths.

claims.title: The shape of the tape
claims.text: At each new cell on the right the tape is 1^3 0 P^n1 Q P^n2 ... Q P^nk 1^8 0 C>0 with P = 150 and Q = 170; the number of blocks grows from 2 to 7 in the first 8.5·108 steps, the last block losing one pair per event. Observed by simulation, not proved.

claims.title: Where it would halt
claims.text: The only halting transition is F reading 0, and F is entered only from E reading 1, so the machine halts exactly when the head in state E reads 1 0 (from the transition table).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1011 steps from blank tape without a halt (377,233 cells visited).

claims.title: Every block is a countdown timer
claims.text: By the digit rules, when digit j goes 1→2 a pair moves from the block after it to the block before it, and when it wraps 3→0 the block before it gains a pair. So the block after digit j loses 2 pairs per cycle of digit j+1 (every 4<sup>j+1</sup> increments) and the first block gains 2 per cycle of the first digit; checked on the run from blank tape (e.g. the second block 13, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3 at consecutive cycles of the second digit, steps 131,121 to 176,267).
claims.where: README, lean/Rules.lean (the rules for the lowest digits)

claims.title: The same tape shape halts with short blocks
claims.text: D> 0 b (ba)^3 a (ba)^3 a 1^4 halts at step 81,375 and D> 0 b (ba)^7 a (ba)^4 a 1^4 at step 227,426 (both of the left-end form seen in the run from blank tape). A nonhalting proof must therefore use the block lengths of the actual run.

claims.title: Many short counter tapes halt
claims.text: Of all tapes of that form with at most two inner separators and blocks 1..4, 142 halt within 10<sup>7</sup> steps; of 200 random ones with up to five inner separators and blocks 2..6, 8 halt within 5·10<sup>7</sup>.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The halt would need the timers to run out in a bad combination (as in the short tapes above); whether the run from blank tape ever produces one is open. The boundary rules (a block running out, the carry off the top, a new digit at the left) are not yet written down.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tape and head as 1RB1RF_1LC1RD_1RA1LD_1RE0LA_---0RC_0LC1RB at every one of the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps (the tables differ). The same table as 1RB1LD_1RC1RE_1LA0RA_1RC0LB_0LA1RF_---1RD up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. Started on a blank tape, this machine counts in base 4 at the left end of its tape; the digits sit between long blocks that each count down like a timer. The digit rules are proved in Lean, and so is the fact that the same kind of tape halts when its timers are short: whether the real run ever gets into such a state is the open question.

facts.text: Proved in Lean for all block lengths.
Two tapes of the same shape with short blocks halt (Lean).
No halt from blank tape in the C simulator.

sections.eyebrow: What the tape is made of
sections.heading: Digits between blocks
html: With the words a = 10, b = 1110, whenever the head is back at the left end the tape reads
D>0 b (ba)^n1 s1 (ba)^n2 s2 ... (ba)^nk sk  [right end]
long blocks of pairs ba separated by digits si, each one of a, b, ab, bb. The head walks to the first digit, changes it, and walks back:

• a → b and ab → bb;
  • b → ab, and one pair ba moves from the block on its right to the block on its left;
  • bb → a with the block on its left one pair longer, and the same step is applied to the next digit (a carry).
So the digits count in base 4 (a = 0, b = 1, ab = 2, bb = 3), while the blocks between them slowly drift. An example run of five increments:

D>0 b (ba)^4 a  (ba)^21 bb (ba)^59 b 1111
D>0 b (ba)^4 b  (ba)^21 bb (ba)^59 b 1111
D>0 b (ba)^5 ab (ba)^20 bb (ba)^59 b 1111
D>0 b (ba)^5 bb (ba)^20 bb (ba)^59 b 1111
D>0 b (ba)^6 a  (ba)^21 a  (ba)^59 b 1111

sections.heading: Every block counts down
html: Number the blocks B0, B1, B2, ... from the left; digit j sits between B(j-1) and Bj. When digit j goes 1→2, one pair moves from Bj to B(j-1); when it wraps 3→0, B(j-1) gains a pair. Over one cycle of digit j+1 (4j+1 increments) Bj gains 2 pairs and loses 4: Bj drops by 2 every 4j+1 increments, while B0 grows by 2 per cycle of the first digit.

stepB0B1B2digit 3
131,12161318a
135,647141118ab
142,30522917bb
152,17730717a
163,13738516b
176,26746316ab
205,76465615b (B1 ran out; the digits are rearranged)

The leftmost block grows by a constant per cycle, and the head crosses it on every increment, so the time per increment grows linearly and the tape's left side grows like the square root of time; the digits themselves, few and slowly changing, make the logarithmic side.

sections.heading: The carry reaches the right end
html: When a carry runs off the last digit the head goes to the right end, which gains a cell. There the tape reads 1110 P^n1 Q P^n2 ... Q P^nk 1^8 0 with P = 150, Q = 170:
The number of digits grows slowly (the right side of the tape grows like the logarithm of time); the blocks, all swept by the head, make the left side grow like its square root.

sections.heading: Open
html: The machine halts exactly when the head in state E reads 1 0. None of the digit rules does that; whether one of the boundary cases (an empty block, the carry at the right end, a new digit at the left end) can is the open part. Decoding those cases would turn the machine into a map on the list of blocks and digits.

sections.heading: Short timers halt
html: Tapes of exactly the same shape halt when their blocks are short. Lean checks two by evaluation:

tapehalts at step
D> 0 b (ba)^3 a (ba)^3 a 1^481,375
D> 0 b (ba)^7 a (ba)^4 a 1^4227,426

In the second one the counter counts normally until every digit is 3 (bb), and the carry off the top runs into the short end and halts. So nothing about the shape of the tape rules a halt out: a proof of nonhalting would have to show that the timers in the run from blank tape never run out in such a combination, an arithmetic question about the block lengths that is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.506). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.063).
After 109 steps the tape spans 57,981 cells (40,782 left of the start, 58 right), with a density of 1s of 0.757.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same run as 1RB1RF_1LC1RD_1RA1LD_1RE0LA_---0RC_0LC1RB (observed, not proved). At every one of the first 107 steps from blank tape the two machines have the same tape and the head on the same cell. Their tables differ, and no renaming of the states turns one into the other. While they run, the states pair up as A–A, B–B, B–E, C–C, D–D, E–F, F–B (this machine first), which is not one to one. Transitions not used in these steps: this machine never uses F0 and the other never uses E0. Lean proves (lean/Twin.lean here, lock_or_break, not_halts_of_noBreak) that the two runs have the same tape, the same head position and paired states up to the first break, a configuration where the paired states act differently, and that neither machine halts if no break ever comes. A halt of either machine is itself a break, and the halting transitions of the two do not correspond, so the two are not known to halt together.

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A base-4 counter (digits a, b, ab, bb) between blocks of pairs ba, each block a countdown timer; digit rules proved in Lean, short-timer tapes of the same shape halt (Lean), no halt in 10^11 steps.
